Summary
Economic viability of drill cuttings valorization depends on whether revenues from reuse (or avoided disposal charges) exceed the sum of collection, conditioning, processing, and transport costs while meeting performance and regulatory requirements; in practice, it often compares against a variable landfill tipping fee baseline rather than a universal fixed cost. Reported cost assessments frequently conflict because studies differ in scope (tipping fee vs. social cost internalization), treatment pathways (e.g., stabilization vs. thermal desorption), local regulations, transport distances, oil content of the feedstock, and accounting of energy and capital, alongside sensitivity to oil price and fiscal regimes. <cite id="758798cf-0">If the treatment technology is not properly selected, it will seriously increase the burden of business operations; economics should consider immediate, disposal, transportation, equipment, and energy costs</cite> <cite id="758798cf-1">Finally, evaluation requires operating performance factors such as safety, processing rate, reliability, and end product condition</cite> <cite id="999d8ece-0">Reuse reduces costs that would otherwise be spent on transporting drill cuttings to disposal sites and paying landfill acceptance charges</cite> <cite id="999d8ece-1">Tipping fees vary widely by site and circumstance; typical ranges are about $10–$120 per ton with local municipal streams lower and long-haul tipping fees higher</cite>.

What determines economic viability
Economic viability must compare incremental revenues and avoided costs of valorization against a credible alternative, typically landfilling under prevailing local fees and logistics. Valorization projects that stabilize, separate, or transform drill cuttings can reduce or avoid disposal charges and create product value, but only if the treated product meets quality and regulatory targets and the total cost (capital, energy, and operations) is justified by market or regulatory revenues. <cite id="999d8ece-0">Reuse lowers transportation and landfill acceptance costs</cite> <cite id="999d8ece-1">Landfill disposal costs depend on land value, capacity, construction/maintenance, and community compensation, with ranges of roughly $10–$120 per ton and local municipal streams often cheaper than industrial hauls</cite>. Transport cost structures also create distance-sensitive economies of scale; for example, one estimate places full-garbage-truck removal costs at about $5.33 per mile, making local aggregation and route optimization pivotal to breakeven. <cite id="999d8ece-1">Transportation costs can dominate over several dollars per mile, and landfilling can be cheapest or most expensive depending on parameters, with typical ranges of $10–$120 per ton</cite>. In oil and gas contexts, broader fiscal and price dynamics affect willingness and ability to invest in valorization: declining crude prices and uncertain project economics raise financing risk and can shift operators toward lower-cost waste handling, while supportive fiscal policy can unlock marginal reserves and parallel investments in cleaner waste pathways. <cite id="758798cf-2">When future oil prices fall below about $50/bbl, development becomes adverse; project expenditures and financing uncertainty challenge alternatives, and fiscal terms (royalties, bonuses) influence investor interest</cite>.

Valorization routes and where they become viable
Multiple reuse pathways exist, each with performance envelopes and cost profiles that determine where they cross economically into viability:

- Stabilization/solidification and re-use in civil infrastructure. Cement-based stabilization and thermal desorption can condition oil-based drill cuttings for use as subbase/base or in concrete, but environmental screening may still require corrective action if target contaminants are not fully immobilized. <cite id="772fef6c-0">Comparing stabilization and solidification to no-treatment and thermal desorption, stabilization/solidification emerged as best approaches with lowest impacts</cite> <cite id="772fef6c-2">For pre-treated oil-based drill cuttings, 2% addition in cement produced UCS of 22.22–26.22 N/mm² above grade-20 concrete minimum (20 N/mm²), yet total petroleum hydrocarbons averaged 62.41 mg/kg, slightly exceeding a 50 mg/kg regulatory target, implying additional corrective action before construction reuse</cite>. If stabilization meets local environmental screening, reuse in base/subbase can be cost-effective by avoiding landfill and meeting geotechnical specs. <cite id="772fef6c-0">Drill cuttings are widely used to stabilize erodible pads and as kiln feed, bricks, concrete blocks, highway construction, and soil fertilizer; stabilization increased unconfined compressive strength, California bearing ratio, and durability in petroleum-contaminated soils treated with cement/lime/fly ash</cite>.

- Incorporation in asphalt and concrete mixes. Small fractions of low-oil-content drill cuttings can be substituted for aggregates or mineral fillers in asphalt concrete, reducing material costs while preserving performance; higher oil contents degrade tensile strength and raise compliance risks. <cite id="772fef6c-1">Massachusetts DEQE permitted replacing 5% aggregate with soil containing 3% oil (gasoline/kerosene), and New Jersey studies allowed up to 35% petroleum-contaminated soil in hot-mix asphalt with tensile strength ratios not meaningfully different from control and hydraulic conductivity below 2×10⁻⁶ cm/s</cite> <cite id="9dd3c197-0">Laboratory studies from Western Siberia showed asphalt concrete mixtures with drill cuttings met regulatory requirements but tensile strength decreased with higher cuttings share, creating discrepancies with some regulatory requirements</cite> <cite id="9dd3c197-2">Oil-based drill cuttings can be recommended for inclusion from 1–6% in asphalt concrete; when combined with bitumen and as filler/mineral powder, compositions can meet GOST with oil content treated as a positive activator, though paving temperature control is critical</cite>. In concrete, partial cement replacement with dried drill cuttings can lower binder cost but reduces compressive strength, requiring mix design compensation. <cite id="772fef6c-1">Replacing 5% cement with dried drill cuttings reduced compressive strength by 10%, indicating design trade-offs to maintain performance</cite>.

- Downstream markets and value streams. Where treated drill cuttings meet quality specs, markets include cement kiln feed, bricks/pavers, ballast, and soil amendments; technical performance and regulatory acceptance are gatekeepers. <cite id="772fef6c-0">Reuse as kiln feed in Portland cement, bricks/concrete blocks, highway construction, wetland substrates, and soil fertilizer has been investigated with demonstrated performance gains after stabilization</cite>. In practice, value is often realized via avoided disposal fees and byproduct revenues (e.g., bitumen reduction or filler value) rather than as a primary commodity, making landfill tipping fees and transport distances critical to breakeven. <cite id="999d8ece-0">By substituting reuse for landfilling, operators avoid transport to disposal and landfill acceptance charges</cite> <cite id="999d8ece-1">Given $10–$120/ton tipping fee ranges, the savings per tonne and optimal haul distances materially influence whether reuse is cheaper than landfill</cite>.

Cross-cutting drivers that shift the viability boundary
- Feedstock characteristics. Oil and gas content, moisture, and metal load determine processing route and cost. Stabilization/thermal desorption and separation clean up hydrocarbons and leachables but add capex, opex, and energy costs; if untreated cuttings can be used on-site as erosion control, upfront costs can be avoided. <cite id="772fef6c-0">Stabilization and solidification were shown to be low-impact options, and drill cuttings are used for erosion control on roads and pads</cite> <cite id="772fef6c-2">Post-cement stabilization still showed residual TPH above a 50 mg/kg target, necessitating corrective action for sustainable reuse</cite>.

- Scale, aggregation, and logistics. Aggregating wastes to support long routes and achieving throughput economies reduces unit transport and disposal costs; municipal or industrial tipping differentials and distance to disposal can flip the economic decision. <cite id="999d8ece-1">Transport costs are significant per mile; landfilling cheapest or most expensive varies with parameters, with $22–$102/ton observed in Washington State; large throughput thresholds (e.g., >100,000 t/y) can make alternatives competitive</cite>.

- Oil price and fiscal regime. Operator incentives and capital availability are sensitive to crude prices and fiscal terms; low oil prices and high taxes can compress budgets and favor lower-cost waste pathways, while supportive policies or tax adjustments can unlock investment in valorization. <cite id="758798cf-2">Below ~$50/bbl, development economics deteriorate; changes in royalty/bonus structures and fiscal terms can increase interest in marginal reserves and associated investments</cite>.

- Environmental and social cost accounting. When social and externality costs of landfilling are capitalized, reuse becomes comparatively more attractive at smaller scales; conversely, if valorization introduces unmanaged risks (e.g., elevated TPH), additional remediation costs appear. <cite id="999d8ece-2">At ~$184/tonne landfill tipping fee, electricity and RNG-from-waste scenarios become attractive above 100,000 t/y throughput; accounting for social costs of landfilling (e.g., $25–40/ton for air pollutant and GHG impacts) further improves competitiveness of valorization alternatives</cite> <cite id="772fef6c-2">Even after stabilization/thermal treatment, slight TPH exceedance implies corrective action costs before construction reuse</cite>.

Why reported cost assessments conflict
Methodological heterogeneity across studies explains divergent cost numbers and conclusions. First, cost scope and accounting differ: some analyses compare reuse to landfill tipping fees while others compare to internal transfer prices or to a “do-nothing” baseline with implicit environmental liabilities; including social costs shifts breakeven. <cite id="999d8ece-2">If social costs of landfilling are monetized, tipping fees need to increase by $25–40/ton and alternative valorization becomes attractive at smaller scales</cite> <cite id="999d8ece-0">Direct savings from avoided transport and landfill acceptance charges can materially alter net costs</cite>. Second, treatment pathways and performance specs vary: stabilization, thermal desorption, cement kiln injection, and mechanical separation have different capex, opex, and yield profiles, and different regulatory acceptance envelopes, with some reuse only allowed within tight oil-content limits. <cite id="772fef6c-0">Stabilization and solidification were identified as low-impact approaches, and oil-based cuttings can be used in bricks/concrete and base/subbase with performance gains after treatment</cite> <cite id="772fef6c-1">Permitted oil contents in asphalt ranges from 3% (by replacing 5% aggregate) up to 35% contaminated soil, with maintained tensile strength and conductivity constraints</cite> <cite id="9dd3c197-0">Higher cuttings share reduced tensile strength and can conflict with regulatory requirements</cite> <cite id="772fef6c-2">Regulatory screening after S/S can require corrective action due to residual TPH</cite>. Third, transport distance, oil price, and local fees are case-specific and highly variable, producing different breakeven thresholds across geographies and operators. <cite id="999d8ece-1">Tipping fees range $10–$120/ton and can be local-municipal low or remote-high; transport costs per mile can be several dollars, altering the economics by haul distance</cite> <cite id="758798cf-2">Oil price below $50/bbl and fiscal terms affect investment and cost comparisons</cite>. Fourth, evaluation frameworks differ: some emphasize technical feasibility and lab performance while underweighting full life-cycle costs and permitting timelines; others emphasize immediate OPEX but neglect capex recovery and working capital. <cite id="758798cf-1">Economic assessments must integrate immediate, disposal, transport, equipment, and energy costs alongside operating performance (safety, reliability, end product condition)</cite>. Finally, uncertainty and sensitivity analyses are inconsistently reported; studies that do not monetize noncompliance risk or downstream remediation liabilities will underestimate costs when regulatory noncompliance occurs. <cite id="772fef6c-2">Even treated and stabilized drill cuttings may fail environmental screening, requiring additional corrective measures that add cost and delay</cite>.

Practical decision rules and design of viable valorization
- Prefer reuse routes with demonstrated compliance and stable specs. Favor stabilization/thermal desorption pathways that meet local screening for construction reuse; if not, consider on-site stabilization (e.g., for pads/roads) to avoid off-site transport and landfill fees. <cite id="772fef6c-0">Stabilization and solidification are low-impact approaches, and stabilized material can be used for erosion control and as base/subbase</cite> <cite id="772fef6c-2">Residual TPH may exceed targets even after S/S, requiring corrective action for construction reuse</cite>.

- Anchor to local disposal costs and transport logistics. Compute breakeven when reuse avoids landfill fees and transport charges; aggregation to support long-haul optimization and achieving high tonnage throughput reduces unit costs. <cite id="999d8ece-0">Reuse saves landfill acceptance and transport to disposal</cite> <cite id="999d8ece-1">Landfill tipping fees range $10–$120/ton; transport costs per mile are material</cite> <cite id="999d8ece-2">Large-scale diversion thresholds (e.g., >100,000 t/y) improve viability; monetizing social costs further improves the case</cite>.

- Engineer for market specs. For asphalt and concrete, target low oil fractions and proven mix designs; if oil is an activator, validate stability and rutting/thermal sensitivity. <cite id="9dd3c197-2">1–6% oil-based cuttings can be included in asphalt concrete with bitumen adjustments and compliance to GOST, though temperature control is critical</cite> <cite id="772fef6c-1">Permitted oil contents and performance metrics differ by jurisdiction and mix design</cite> <cite id="9dd3c197-0">Tensile strength decreases with higher cuttings share, requiring compliance-conscious limits</cite>.

- Internalize policy and fiscal context. Where oil prices are low or royalties/high, prioritize least-regret valorization routes; where policy supports waste diversion or credits, capture them in TEA. <cite id="758798cf-2">Oil price below $50/bbl and fiscal terms materially affect development and willingness to invest in waste management pathways</cite> <cite id="999d8ece-2">Accounting for social costs of landfilling increases the attractiveness of diversion/valorization at smaller scales</cite>.

- Do sensitivity analysis around oil content, moisture, energy prices, and fees. Report breakeven ranges versus landfill tipping fee and haul distance, and include a noncompliance risk budget for regulatory screening. <cite id="758798cf-1">Economic evaluation must include transport, disposal, equipment, and energy costs</cite> <cite id="772fef6c-2">Regulatory noncompliance risk can trigger corrective costs even after stabilization</cite>.

Evidence sufficiency and remaining gaps
The literature supports that valorization is economically viable when treated products meet regulatory performance and quality specs and when avoided disposal costs and product revenues exceed the sum of collection, conditioning, and processing costs; viability is highly sensitive to local tipping fees, transport distances, feedstock oil content, and fiscal context. <cite id="758798cf-0">Economics should consider immediate, disposal, transportation, equipment, and energy costs</cite> <cite id="772fef6c-0">Stabilization/solidification reduce impacts and enable reuse in roads, bricks, concrete, and asphalt</cite> <cite id="999d8ece-0">Reuse directly reduces transport and landfill acceptance charges</cite> <cite id="999d8ece-1">Tipping fees span $10–$120/ton with strong distance and locality effects</cite> <cite id="758798cf-2">Oil price and fiscal terms shift the investment calculus</cite>. Reported cost assessments conflict primarily because of differences in baseline (tipping fees vs. internal costs), treatment pathways, regulatory acceptance envelopes, transport logistics, and whether social/externality costs are monetized; harmonizing these inputs and reporting sensitivity ranges resolves many discrepancies. <cite id="999d8ece-2">Monetizing social costs of landfilling narrows the gap and improves valorization competitiveness</cite> <cite id="772fef6c-2">Post-treatment screening failures add hidden remediation costs</cite> <cite id="758798cf-1">Operational performance criteria and cost categories influence outcomes</cite>.

Practical takeaway
Valorization is economically viable when: (1) treated cuttings meet market and regulatory specs at predictable quality; (2) local tipping fees and transport logistics are unfavorable enough to make reuse savings material; (3) operators achieve throughput and scale to spread capex and haul costs; and (4) fiscal/policy conditions support diversion investments. <cite id="772fef6c-0">Stabilization and reuse in subbase/construction are feasible when performance thresholds are met</cite> <cite id="999d8ece-1">Given $10–$120/ton tipping fee ranges and multi-dollar-per-mile transport costs, short hauls and diversion can flip the economics</cite> <cite id="758798cf-2">Favorable fiscal policy and higher oil prices increase willingness and feasibility of valorization investments</cite>. Summary
Economic viability of drill cuttings valorization depends on whether revenues from reuse (or avoided disposal charges) exceed the sum of collection, conditioning, processing, and transport costs while meeting performance and regulatory requirements; in practice, it often compares against a variable landfill tipping fee baseline rather than a universal fixed cost. Reported cost assessments frequently conflict because studies differ in scope (tipping fee vs. social cost internalization), treatment pathways (e.g., stabilization vs. thermal desorption), local regulations, transport distances, oil content of the feedstock, and accounting of energy and capital, alongside sensitivity to oil price and fiscal regimes. <cite id="758798cf-0">If the treatment technology is not properly selected, it will seriously increase the burden of business operations; economics should consider immediate, disposal, transportation, equipment, and energy costs</cite> <cite id="758798cf-1">Finally, evaluation requires operating performance factors such as safety, processing rate, reliability, and end product condition</cite> <cite id="999d8ece-0">Reuse reduces costs that would otherwise be spent on transporting drill cuttings to disposal sites and paying landfill acceptance charges</cite> <cite id="999d8ece-1">Tipping fees vary widely by site and circumstance; typical ranges are about $10–$120 per ton with local municipal streams lower and long-haul tipping fees higher</cite>.

What determines economic viability
Economic viability must compare incremental revenues and avoided costs of valorization against a credible alternative, typically landfilling under prevailing local fees and logistics. Valorization projects that stabilize, separate, or transform drill cuttings can reduce or avoid disposal charges and create product value, but only if the treated product meets quality and regulatory targets and the total cost (capital, energy, and operations) is justified by market or regulatory revenues. <cite id="999d8ece-0">Reuse lowers transportation and landfill acceptance costs</cite> <cite id="999d8ece-1">Landfill disposal costs depend on land value, capacity, construction/maintenance, and community compensation, with ranges of roughly $10–$120 per ton and local municipal streams often cheaper than industrial hauls</cite>. Transport cost structures also create distance-sensitive economies of scale; for example, one estimate places full-garbage-truck removal costs at about $5.33 per mile, making local aggregation and route optimization pivotal to breakeven. <cite id="999d8ece-1">Transportation costs can dominate over several dollars per mile, and landfilling can be cheapest or most expensive depending on parameters, with typical ranges of $10–$120 per ton</cite>. In oil and gas contexts, broader fiscal and price dynamics affect willingness and ability to invest in valorization: declining crude prices and uncertain project economics raise financing risk and can shift operators toward lower-cost waste handling, while supportive fiscal policy can unlock marginal reserves and parallel investments in cleaner waste pathways. <cite id="758798cf-2">When future oil prices fall below about $50/bbl, development becomes adverse; project expenditures and financing uncertainty challenge alternatives, and fiscal terms (royalties, bonuses) influence investor interest</cite>.

Valorization routes and where they become viable
Multiple reuse pathways exist, each with performance envelopes and cost profiles that determine where they cross economically into viability:

- Stabilization/solidification and re-use in civil infrastructure. Cement-based stabilization and thermal desorption can condition oil-based drill cuttings for use as subbase/base or in concrete, but environmental screening may still require corrective action if target contaminants are not fully immobilized. <cite id="772fef6c-0">Comparing stabilization and solidification to no-treatment and thermal desorption, stabilization/solidification emerged as best approaches with lowest impacts</cite> <cite id="772fef6c-2">For pre-treated oil-based drill cuttings, 2% addition in cement produced UCS of 22.22–26.22 N/mm² above grade-20 concrete minimum (20 N/mm²), yet total petroleum hydrocarbons averaged 62.41 mg/kg, slightly exceeding a 50 mg/kg regulatory target, implying additional corrective action before construction reuse</cite>. If stabilization meets local environmental screening, reuse in base/subbase can be cost-effective by avoiding landfill and meeting geotechnical specs. <cite id="772fef6c-0">Drill cuttings are widely used to stabilize erodible pads and as kiln feed, bricks, concrete blocks, highway construction, and soil fertilizer; stabilization increased unconfined compressive strength, California bearing ratio, and durability in petroleum-contaminated soils treated with cement/lime/fly ash</cite>.

- Incorporation in asphalt and concrete mixes. Small fractions of low-oil-content drill cuttings can be substituted for aggregates or mineral fillers in asphalt concrete, reducing material costs while preserving performance; higher oil contents degrade tensile strength and raise compliance risks. <cite id="772fef6c-1">Massachusetts DEQE permitted replacing 5% aggregate with soil containing 3% oil (gasoline/kerosene), and New Jersey studies allowed up to 35% petroleum-contaminated soil in hot-mix asphalt with tensile strength ratios not meaningfully different from control and hydraulic conductivity below 2×10⁻⁶ cm/s</cite> <cite id="9dd3c197-0">Laboratory studies from Western Siberia showed asphalt concrete mixtures with drill cuttings met regulatory requirements but tensile strength decreased with higher cuttings share, creating discrepancies with some regulatory requirements</cite> <cite id="9dd3c197-2">Oil-based drill cuttings can be recommended for inclusion from 1–6% in asphalt concrete; when combined with bitumen and as filler/mineral powder, compositions can meet GOST with oil content treated as a positive activator, though paving temperature control is critical</cite>. In concrete, partial cement replacement with dried drill cuttings can lower binder cost but reduces compressive strength, requiring mix design compensation. <cite id="772fef6c-1">Replacing 5% cement with dried drill cuttings reduced compressive strength by 10%, indicating design trade-offs to maintain performance</cite>.

- Downstream markets and value streams. Where treated drill cuttings meet quality specs, markets include cement kiln feed, bricks/pavers, ballast, and soil amendments; technical performance and regulatory acceptance are gatekeepers. <cite id="772fef6c-0">Reuse as kiln feed in Portland cement, bricks/concrete blocks, highway construction, wetland substrates, and soil fertilizer has been investigated with demonstrated performance gains after stabilization</cite>. In practice, value is often realized via avoided disposal fees and byproduct revenues (e.g., bitumen reduction or filler value) rather than as a primary commodity, making landfill tipping fees and transport distances critical to breakeven. <cite id="999d8ece-0">By substituting reuse for landfilling, operators avoid transport to disposal and landfill acceptance charges</cite> <cite id="999d8ece-1">Given $10–$120/ton tipping fee ranges, the savings per tonne and optimal haul distances materially influence whether reuse is cheaper than landfill</cite>.

- Feedstock characteristics. Oil and gas content, moisture, and metal load determine processing route and cost. Stabilization/thermal desorption and separation clean up hydrocarbons and leachables but add capex, opex, and energy costs; if untreated cuttings can be used on-site as erosion control, upfront costs can be avoided. <cite id="772fef6c-0">Stabilization and solidification were shown to be low-impact options, and drill cuttings are used for erosion control on roads and pads</cite> <cite id="772fef6c-2">Post-cement stabilization still showed residual TPH above a 50 mg/kg target, necessitating corrective action for sustainable reuse</cite>.

- Scale, aggregation, and logistics. Aggregating wastes to support long routes and achieving throughput economies reduces unit transport and disposal costs; municipal or industrial tipping differentials and distance to disposal can flip the economic decision. <cite id="999d8ece-1">Transport costs are significant per mile; landfilling cheapest or most expensive varies with parameters, with $22–$102/ton observed in Washington State; large throughput thresholds (e.g., >100,000 t/y) can make alternatives competitive</cite>.

- Oil price and fiscal regime. Operator incentives and capital availability are sensitive to crude prices and fiscal terms; low oil prices and high taxes can compress budgets and favor lower-cost waste pathways, while supportive policies or tax adjustments can unlock investment in valorization. <cite id="758798cf-2">Below ~$50/bbl, development economics deteriorate; changes in royalty/bonus structures and fiscal terms can increase interest in marginal reserves and associated investments</cite>.

Why reported cost assessments conflict
Methodological heterogeneity across studies explains divergent cost numbers and conclusions. First, cost scope and accounting differ: some analyses compare reuse to landfill tipping fees while others compare to internal transfer prices or to a “do-nothing” baseline with implicit environmental liabilities; including social costs shifts breakeven. <cite id="999d8ece-2">If social costs of landfilling are monetized, tipping fees need to increase by $25–40/ton and alternative valorization becomes attractive at smaller scales</cite> <cite id="999d8ece-0">Direct savings from avoided transport and landfill acceptance charges can materially alter net costs</cite>. Second, treatment pathways and performance specs vary: stabilization, thermal desorption, cement kiln injection, and mechanical separation have different capex, opex, and yield profiles, and different regulatory acceptance envelopes, with some reuse only allowed within tight oil-content limits. <cite id="772fef6c-0">Stabilization and solidification were identified as low-impact approaches, and oil-based cuttings can be used in bricks/concrete and base/subbase with performance gains after treatment</cite> <cite id="772fef6c-1">Permitted oil contents in asphalt ranges from 3% (by replacing 5% aggregate) up to 35% contaminated soil, with maintained tensile strength and conductivity constraints</cite> <cite id="9dd3c197-0">Higher cuttings share reduced tensile strength and can conflict with regulatory requirements</cite> <cite id="772fef6c-2">Regulatory screening after S/S can require corrective action due to residual TPH</cite>. Third, transport distance, oil price, and local fees are case-specific and highly variable, producing different breakeven thresholds across geographies and operators. <cite id="999d8ece-1">Tipping fees range $10–$120/ton and can be local-municipal low or remote-high; transport costs per mile can be several dollars, altering the economics by haul distance</cite> <cite id="758798cf-2">Oil price below $50/bbl and fiscal terms affect investment and cost comparisons</cite>. Fourth, evaluation frameworks differ: some emphasize technical feasibility and lab performance while underweighting full life-cycle costs and permitting timelines; others emphasize immediate OPEX but neglect capex recovery and working capital. <cite id="758798cf-1">Economic assessments must integrate immediate, disposal, transport, equipment, and energy costs alongside operating performance (safety, reliability, end product condition)</cite>. Practical decision rules and design of viable valorization
- Prefer reuse routes with demonstrated compliance and stable specs. Favor stabilization/thermal desorption pathways that meet local screening for construction reuse; if not, consider on-site stabilization (e.g., for pads/roads) to avoid off-site transport and landfill fees. <cite id="772fef6c-0">Stabilization and solidification are low-impact approaches, and stabilized material can be used for erosion control and as base/subbase</cite> <cite id="772fef6c-2">Residual TPH may exceed targets even after S/S, requiring corrective action for construction reuse</cite>.

Compute breakeven when reuse avoids landfill fees and transport charges; aggregation to support long-haul optimization and achieving high tonnage throughput reduces unit costs. <cite id="999d8ece-0">Reuse saves landfill acceptance and transport to disposal</cite> <cite id="999d8ece-1">Landfill tipping fees range $10–$120/ton; transport costs per mile are material</cite> <cite id="999d8ece-2">Large-scale diversion thresholds (e.g., >100,000 t/y) improve viability; monetizing social costs further improves the case</cite>.

Title: Feasibility Study of the Potential Use of Drill Cuttings in Concrete
Snippet: The life cycle assessment of this study contained different stabilization and treatment systems such as reserve pit without treatment and solidification and thermal desorption. Comparing different scenarios for the treatment, they showed that stabilization and solidification are the best approaches and have the lowest impacts. 

In recent years, many researchers have studied the stabilization of hazardous waste [6][7][8]. In a parallel recent trend, researchers have begun to investigate the incorporation of recycling drill cuttings in various applications such as using them as a kiln feed in the manufacture of Portland cement [9,10], in the manufacture of bricks and concrete blocks [10,11], highway construction [12,13], as substrate in wetlands restoration [14][15][16][17], and soil fertilizer [18]. One wide spread application of drill cuttings is to stabilize areas that are susceptible to getting eroded such as roads and drilling pads [13]. 

In a study conducted by Tuncan et al. [13], petroleum-contaminated soil was stabilized with 5% cement, 10% fly ash, and 20% lime, so it can be used as a sub-base material for road construction. These mixtures were found to be effective and safe for using as a sub-base material. Laboratory studies showed a significant increase in the unconfined compressive strength, California bearing ratio, and durability. However, a similar decrease was obtained in electrical, conductivity and cation exchange capacity. In another study performed by Li et al. [19], the effect of diesel based drilling fluids on Portland cement was investigated. They examined the mechanism of contracting cement slurry and diesel based fluid materials which lead to the contamination mitigation. Results showed that the changes in the slurry properties were caused by osmotic pressure and demulsification. Having investigated the physical and chemical properties of drill cuttings, several studies have attempted to use petroleum-contaminated soil in hot mix asphalt concrete. In a study conducted in Massachusetts Department of Environmental Quality and Engineering, it was permitted to replace 5% of the aggregate in hot mix asphalt with soil containing 3% of oil, gasoline, or kerosene [20].

Title: Feasibility Study of the Potential Use of Drill Cuttings in Concrete
Snippet: In a study conducted in Massachusetts Department of Environmental Quality and Engineering, it was permitted to replace 5% of the aggregate in hot mix asphalt with soil containing 3% of oil, gasoline, or kerosene [20]. In another study, Meegoda and Muller [21] examined the integration of petroleum-contaminated soil into hot mix asphalt concrete in New Jersey. It was found that it is possible to include up to 35% petroleum-contaminated soil in the mix. Later, Meegoda et al. [22] revealed that the tensile strength ratio for hot mix asphalt containing petroleum-contaminated soil was not meaningfully different from the control mix. Their results indicated that saturated hydraulic conductivity values of all hot mix asphalt samples containing petroleum-contaminated soil were less than 2× 10 6 cm/s. In a similar study, Aydilek et al. [23] mixed fly ash with drilling waste to be used as base or sub-base material. Fly ash can be used as mineral filler in hot mix asphalt paving applications. Their results showed that fly ash is a good additive to reduce leaching. 

Taha et al. [24] studied the possible application of bottom sludge from petroleum tanks as paving materials in roads. In their study, the total petroleum hydrocarbon contents were as high as 50 to 65%. Hot mix asphalt specimens containing petroleum waste were created by blending the heated sludge and aggregates without the addition of fresh asphalt. Different sludge percentages, ranging between 3% and 7% were added to the clean aggregate. Test results showed a noteworthy increase in stability with the addition up to 5% of sludge, followed by a stability decrease upon further increase in sludge content. 

The present study investigates the potential of using drill cuttings in concrete as a partial replacement of cement. The innovation of this study is not only to produce a new and cost-effective material from drill cuttings, but also to mitigate its negative environmental impacts. To achieve this objective, laboratory studies were conducted to quantify the compressive strength of concrete samples and to determine the chemical composition of drill cuttings. Results revealed that replacing 5% of cement with dried drill cuttings reduces the compressive strength of concrete by 10%.

Title: Diagnostic screening of organic contaminant level in solidified/stabilized pre-treated oil-based drill cuttings
Snippet: In this study, the diagnostic screening against local environmental guidelines of levels of target contaminants in cement-based solidified/ stabilized low-temperature thermally desorbed oil-based drill cuttings was carried out. This was done to ascertain whether or not some form of action may be required to avert future problems that may arise from the use of solidified/stabilized pre-treated oil-based drill cuttings for construction purposes. Results obtained showed that the 2 % drill cuttings addition yielded the highest UCS (22.22-26.22 N/mm 2 ) at water-tocement ratio of 0.6:1, which were well above the recommended minimum UCS of 20 N/mm 2 for a grade-20 concrete. The average amount of TPH remaining after cement-based S/S of the pre-treated oil-based drill cuttings was 62.41 mg/kg, which slightly exceeded the local regulatory target value of 50 mg/kg. This suggests that cement-based S/S failed to immobilize completely all the hydrocarbons in the pre-treated oil-based drill cuttings. Similarly, there were relics of heavy metals (albeit less than regulatory target values) in the solidified/stabilized matrix. This implies that the solidified/stabilized matrix is not in compliance with environmental guidelines on TPH for sustainable reuse of the pre-treated oilbased drill cuttings as construction materials. As a result, before putting the solidified/stabilized pre-treated oil-based drill cuttings to the intended use, some form of corrective action is required due to the potential environmental health risks of exposure to petroleum hydrocarbons.

Title: Development of a Method for Minimizing the Negative Environmental Impact of Drill Cuttings by Using It as a Mineral Powder in Asphalt Concrete
Snippet: The article describes the problem of environmental pollution from the placement of drill cuttings in it. The main sources of contamination are oil products included in the drill cuttings, chemicals added to the drilling fluid, and heavy metals. In order to reduce the negative impact, it was proposed to use the resource potential of drill cuttings as a mineral powder in the technology for producing asphalt concrete. Samples of drill cuttings were taken in the fields of Western Siberia. It has been established that there are no excesses in the standards for the content of heavy metals in mobile form in samples of drill cuttings. The analysis of physical and chemical characteristics showed that there are high values of COD, oil content, dry residue, rigidity, magnesium and calcium ions, chlorides. Laboratory studies have shown the possibility of using drill cuttings as a mineral powder in asphalt concrete. The optimum composition of the asphalt mixture was obtained. The obtained physical and mechanical properties of asphalt concrete samples comply with the requirements of regulatory documents. It is established that the strength characteristics depend on the percentage of drill cuttings in asphalt concrete: with an increase in the share of drill cuttings, the value of the tensile strength decreases, and at the same time there is a discrepancy with regulatory requirements.

Title: The use of waste in the composition of organic-mineral mixtures used in road construction
Snippet: Drilling cuttings formed during drilling of oil fields can be considered as a raw material for the production of mineral powder for asphalt concrete. The content of oil in drill cuttings is considered a positive factor and can be used to produce activated mineral powder. Such use makes it possible to reduce the amount of bitumen in the asphalt concrete composition and to obtain significant savings in material resources. The studies carried out have shown that the composition of the asphalt concrete mixture: sand -12.5%; crushed stone -45.5%; crushing screening -36%; drill cuttings -6%; bitumen -5.3% over 100% meet the requirements of GOST. Oil-based drill cuttings can be recommended for inclusion in the composition of asphalt concrete from 1 to 6%. 

Waste plastics HDPE and LDPE can be considered as reinforcing and modifying elements in the structure of asphalt concrete. Asphalt concrete, which includes: crushed stone of fraction 10-20 mm -46%; sand -12%; sand from crushing screenings -39%; mineral powder -3%; bitumen BND 60/90 -5% and plastic waste 4% meet the requirements of GOST for asphalt concrete. When using such an asphalt concrete mixture, it is necessary to strictly maintain the paving temperature, since a decrease in temperature sharply increases the rigidity of the mixture, reducing the compaction coefficient of the asphalt concrete. 

Drilling waste and plastic waste have a positive effect on the processes of structure formation in organomineral mixtures. With their help, it is possible to obtain asphalt concrete with increased physical, mechanical and operational performance.
